title: Chamomile tincture for nervous digestion
subtitle: The gut-anxiety cup, concentrated
excerpt: A folk-method chamomile tincture made from dried flowers macerated in 40% vodka for four to six weeks. Traditionally used for the gut-anxiety connection: a nervous stomach, cramping linked to stress, and digestive upset that arrives in tense moments. Two to four ml in a little water, up to three times a day.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), chamomile entry: documents the nervine and carminative uses of chamomile, including for nervous and spasmodic digestive conditions. Felter and Lloyd, King's American Dispensatory (1898): chamomile tincture ratios and dosing in the Eclectic tradition. BHP (1983) chamomile monograph: modern dosing reference for tincture. EMA HMPC monograph on Matricariae flos (2015): safety summary, allergen note for Asteraceae.

recipe.yieldDescription: Approx. 100 ml tincture (about 25 doses at 4 ml)
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tincture macerates for 4 to 6 weeks before it is ready. Finished tincture stores in a dark glass dropper bottle in a cool dark cupboard for up to 2 years.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in an amber glass dropper bottle in a cool dark cupboard. The finished tincture keeps for up to 2 years. Discard if the colour fades noticeably or the smell becomes stale.

projectSchedule.title: Start the maceration
projectSchedule.body: Weigh out 20 g of dried chamomile flowers and put them in a clean 250 ml glass jar with a tight-fitting lid. Pour over 100 ml of 40% ABV plain vodka, making sure the flowers are fully submerged. Seal the jar and label it with today's date. Put it in a cool, dark cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Check the liquid covers the herb
projectSchedule.body: Open the jar and check that the chamomile flowers are still below the surface of the vodka. If the flowers have swollen and are poking above the liquid, top up with a little more vodka just to cover. Give the jar a shake, reseal it, and put it back in the cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Taste check
projectSchedule.body: Dip a clean spoon into the liquid and taste a few drops. By four weeks the tincture should smell clearly of chamomile and have a pleasant, slightly bitter, floral taste. If it tastes weak or thin, leave it another two weeks. Reseal and return it to the cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Strain and bottle
projectSchedule.body: Pour the macerated herb and liquid through muslin cloth set over a measuring jug, squeezing the cloth firmly to get every drop of liquid out. Use a small funnel to decant the finished tincture into a clean amber glass dropper bottle. Label with the herb, the date, and the alcohol percentage. The tincture is now ready to use.

content.text: Chamomile alcohol extract is a concentrated alcohol extract. Dried chamomile flowers soak in 40% vodka for four to six weeks. Unlike the everyday chamomile infusion (made for a general unsettled stomach, Mild colic, or a restless evening), this alcohol extract is in particular for the gut-anxiety link: a nervous stomach, cramping that tightens in stressful moments, and digestive unease that arrives alongside worry rather than after food. The alcohol extract is deep amber-gold and smells strongly of chamomile. At 1 part dried flowers to 5 parts spirit by weight. A 100 ml batch makes around 25 doses and keeps for up to 2 years in a dark glass dropper bottle.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. Allergen note: chamomile belongs to the daisy family (Asteraceae). Readers with a known ragweed or daisy allergy should try a small skin test first chamomile preparations. A reaction to chamomile tea is the usual first indicator. Sedative note: chamomile extract has mild sedating properties. Speak to your prescriber before combining with sleeping tablets or anxiety medication. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: chamomile at culinary-tea strength is widely used in pregnancy. This is a concentrated preparation. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using it in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Do not use herbal preparations in children under twelve without guidance from a herbalist or paediatric doctor.

content.text: Ingredients
This is the folk-method ratio: 1 part dried herb to 5 parts spirit by weight. The 20 g of dried flowers and 100 ml of vodka give approximately 100 ml of finished
alcohol extract
after straining.
Method
Day 0: start the
soaking
Weigh 20 g of dried chamomile flowers into a clean 250 ml glass jar with a tight-fitting lid.
Pour over 100 ml of plain 40% vodka. The flowers should be fully submerged; press them down gently with a clean spoon if needed.
Seal the jar, label it with today's date and the herb name, and place it in a cool dark cupboard.
Day 14: check the liquid
Open the jar and check the flowers are still covered by the vodka. If they have swollen and sit above the surface, top up with a little more vodka to cover. Reseal and return to the cupboard.
Day 28: taste check
Taste a few drops from a clean spoon. The
alcohol extract
should smell clearly of chamomile and have a pleasant, slightly bitter, floral taste. If it seems thin or weak, leave it another two weeks.
Day 42: strain and bottle
Set a double layer of muslin cloth over a measuring jug and pour the
soaking
through it. Gather the corners of the muslin and squeeze firmly to extract every drop.
Use a small funnel to decant the
alcohol extract
into a clean, dry amber glass dropper bottle.
Label with the herb name, the date strained, and '40% vodka
alcohol extract
'. The
alcohol extract
is ready to use.
Dosing

Two to four ml stirred into a small glass of water, up to three times a day. Take before or after meals when digestive symptoms are present. For a course: up to four weeks. Take a two-week break before starting another course. Do not take long-term without review by a herbalist.
Storage
Store in a clean amber glass dropper bottle in a cool dark cupboard. A 40% vodka
alcohol extract
keeps well for up to 2 years. Discard if the colour fades significantly or the smell becomes stale or off.
When not to use this remedy
See a doctor for indigestion that wakes you at night, comes with unexplained weight loss. Painful swallowing, vomiting, black or tarry stools, or chest pain that radiates to the arm or jaw.

Do not use if you have a known allergy to chamomile, daisies, ragweed, or chrysanthemums. Do not use in children under twelve without specialist guidance. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

items.symptom: Tincture is very pale and almost odourless after 6 weeks
items.cause: Dried chamomile flowers were old or poorly stored before use
items.fix: Start a new batch with fresh dried flowers. Good chamomile should smell strongly of the herb and look golden-yellow when dry. Thin, faded flowers produce a thin tincture.

items.symptom: Flowers above the liquid surface after a few days
items.cause: The flowers swelled as they absorbed the alcohol
items.fix: Top up with a little more vodka to keep the flowers submerged. Exposed plant material above the liquid line can go mouldy.
